Hey! My name is /u/Floodgate, and welcome to jackass UrbanExploration.

I'll get the ball rolling with a few important reminders for any first-time UrbExers out there:

  1. Bring GOOD flashlights. No, your phone probably isn't bright enough, nor is it built for constant use. As well, you're going to want it in case of emergency, and flashlights kill phone batteries. Don't bother with dollar-store flashlights. Spend the extra few bucks (20-30) for a decent, quality flashlight and you won't regret it.
  2. Gloves. It's going to get dirty. It's going to get sharp. It's going to get dangerous. Wear thick work gloves to protect your hands from getting cut up.
  3. Boots. Waterproof is good, but boots in general are worth it.
  4. (You probably don't need a) ventilator. Having one on hand can be useful, but generally speaking, you won't need one. Guys that wear gas masks are doing it for show. A decent ventilator can at least save your lungs from heavy dust, or, worst case, asbestos.
  5. Pants/long sleeve shirt. Same reason for gloves, keeping in mind there's a good chance you'll get scratched. Better to sweat and be gross than to be cut up and be grosser.

You probably shouldn't bring: 1. A crowbar 2. Lockpicking kit 3. Hammers 4. Other miscellaneous tools 5. Drugs/alcohol 6. Spray-paint

Depending on your state/province, having a lockpicking kit can get you in jail without question. Check your local laws. Having tools on hand just makes you look unbelievably suspicious, and having drugs/alcohol/paint on your person doesn't help. Just a camera and your clothes will probably make people act a little kinder

Leave it the way you found it. In fact, try to avoid touching in general, but use your best judgement. Don't wreck shit, it'll just ruin someone's day.

Be careful who you share a location to. Nothing's worse than your cool spot getting torched to the ground by everyone finding out about it and tagging the shit out of it.

If you're taking photos, do yourself a favour and take your exterior shots last. Doing it first runs the risk of you getting caught. Get in quickly and quietly, and then take your time. Be aware of your surroundings. Don't get lost in the camera settings. You'll always be able to take the shot another day.

Don't forget: HDR the shit out of every single photo. It only makes it look really cool.

Those of you who are able to lane split, if you've owned both a sport bike and a cruiser, which do you prefer to lane split with during your commute?

I commute 35 miles each way on a supersport and am looking at few things, getting the opinion of those who have done it will help me choose my next bike.
Lane splitting commuters: Standard or Cruiser

The best bike I've ever had for commuting / lane splitting, which is legal here in Northern CA, was an SV650. It was very, very underpowered compared to what I'm used to. But commuting in the bay area (read : giant hills and shitloads of stop and go traffic) the torque was priceless, and it's a relatively narrow bike because of the engine configuration so putting it down the white lines was very easy.

If I lived back in CO I dont think I'd really like it, but for urban commuting it was an excellent bike.

The tried and true SV650 should be considered as well. I'll need to pick out a few bikes and narrow down which have ABS, then see which has better gas mileage, then pick the top few and go check them out in person. That might be the easiest way to go about it.

A standard or sport bike are all better for lane splitting than a cruiser, due to far better handling.

However, a standard 500cc or less is better than a 600cc or greater sport bike, due to the fact standards are much thinner from my experience. I had a Ninja 500 and a CBR 600, and the Ninja was far more easy to handle and maneuver between cars.

Right now I ride a CBR1000RR and can get between cars no problem in San Francisco.
